name: Descriptor + Identifier Label
pattern: NP[descriptor + identifier: number, letter name, or alphanumeric code]

entry.name: Descriptor + Identifier Label
entry.pattern: NP[descriptor + identifier: number, letter name, or alphanumeric code]

1.definition: Identifies a bearer by an assigned label within a naming system.
1.details: The descriptor gives the kind of bearer. The following identifier picks out a bearer within the relevant naming system. Gen in Gen Z supplies the kind in the same way as Ward in CGEL’s Ward 17. Descriptor describes a contribution within the naming construction. In CGEL an embellishment is a semantically nonrestrictive dependent accompanying a proper name. The shared pattern leaves the syntactic head and the identifier’s word category open.

examples.note: Cornell gives these two designations for the same space in Appel Commons.

grounds.locator: Info Session Locations, Appel Commons Community Center

examples.note: Gen identifies the referent as a generation and Z supplies its conventional label. Cohort boundaries can vary across sources.

relatedConstructions.notes: Room 302A realizes naming through a type-denoting descriptor and an assigned code. The identification depends on the code assignment at the relevant site.
Room 101 and Kim both occur as bare argument NPs. In Room 101 the noun supplies the type of bearer and the assigned code supplies its identity.

Dr Patel also places a nominal before an identifying form. Dr is an appellation giving the bearer’s status in a personal name. Room in Room 101 gives the type of entity and the following code is interpreted within the site.

Compare Room 101 with the river Wye. Both pair a type expression with an identifier. The latter has an overt determiner and is analyzed as an integrated appositive. The comparison leaves the headedness of Room 101 open.

grounds.note: Lists Ward 17 among names with a descriptor that indicates the kind of entity named.

Calls Room an embellishment rather than an attributive modifier (n. 9). The wider construction uses CGEL’s descriptor for the type-denoting element, and CGEL’s embellishments include nominal attributive modifiers (p. 520).

projection.target: A descriptor can be followed by a number, a letter or a mixed code in the same naming role. Changing a label may change the bearer, or leave it fixed if the two labels are aliases. Any quantity or rank associated with the code depends on the local allocation convention.
projection.evidence: Cornell uses Room 101 and Room 302A, and gives Multipurpose Room A for the same space as Room 302A. CGEL gives Ward 17. Pew uses Gen Z as a cohort label.

known_boundary_items: In 101 rooms, 101 determines how many rooms. In Room 101, it identifies a room.
In a type specification such as a type A personality, the designation supplies a class inside an ordinary count NP. Compare bare Gen Z for an identified cohort.

curious.title: A kind of thing plus its label
curious.summary: A word naming a kind of thing, followed by a number or letter code, can pick out one particular thing.
curious.body:
Many names are built from two parts: a word that says what kind of thing it is, and a label that says which one. In Room 302A, Room gives the kind and 302A is the label. In Gen Z, Gen tells you it's a generation and Z is its label.

The label can be a number, a letter or a mix of both. What the label means depends on the system it belongs to. A university, for instance, can give the same space two designations, Room 302A and Multipurpose Room A. Changing the label might change which thing you mean, unless the two labels are just different names for the same thing.
curious.try: Think of a place you know that has a kind word plus a code, like a room, a gate or a ward. Does the code tell you anything beyond "this one"?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why Room 302A and Gen Z are naming patterns, not descriptions with a number or letter attached.
teacher.explain: These names pair a descriptor (the word giving the kind of bearer, such as Room or Gen) with an identifier (a number, letter name or mixed code) that picks out a bearer within a naming system. The same pattern covers Ward 17, Room 302A and Gen Z. In CGEL, an embellishment is a semantically nonrestrictive dependent accompanying a proper name. This dictionary leaves open which element is the syntactic head and what word category the identifier has. Any quantity or rank the code suggests depends on how the codes were allocated locally. Contrast 101 rooms, where 101 counts rooms, with Room 101, where it identifies one.
teacher.terms: Descriptor: CGEL's term for the element that indicates the kind of entity named, as in Ward 17. Embellishment: CGEL's term for a nonrestrictive dependent accompanying a proper name.

contrasts.note: The number says how many rooms.

watch_for: A learner might read Room 302A as a count or ranking of rooms rather than a label for one room.
A learner might treat Gen Z as a description of a person's character rather than as the label for a generation.
teacher.activity: Students collect descriptor-plus-code names from their school or neighbourhood (rooms, buses, forms, teams), then sort the codes into numbers, letters and mixed codes and say what kind each code names.
